culture-and-protocol.dress_and_conduct: Ghana Tourism Authority: tipping is permitted and rarely added to the bill, so let the service guide what you give waiters, taxi drivers, porters and guides; pack light, washable cotton and casual clothing. Ghana is conservative and deeply religious: dress modestly and respect traditional values. Wearing military clothing, including camouflage, is illegal. Carry ID (a copy of the photo page is fine). Even small amounts of cannabis can bring more than 5 years in prison. Do not photograph military sites or the airport; ask before photographing guarded buildings.

visa-preparation.entry_summary: A visa is needed. The Ghana Immigration Service eVisa covers tourism and business: apply online, pay, and receive the single-entry eVisa by email. A yellow fever certificate is required on arrival.
visa-preparation.fastest_entry: Single-entry eVisa through the official Ghana Immigration Service portal; standard processing 96 hours (express 5 hours for a higher fee).
visa-preparation.before_departure: Check eligibility on the eVisa portal, apply with photo and supporting documents, pay, answer any request for information within 3 days, and travel within the eVisa's 90-day validity. Carry the yellow fever certificate.
visa-preparation.useful_stay: The eVisa is valid 90 days from issue for one entry; the immigration officer sets the stay, up to 60 days. Staying more than 90 days in a year requires a Non-citizen Ghanacard.

steps.step: Check eligibility and apply for the eVisa (tourist or business) on the official portal.
Upload the photo and supporting documents, pay the fee for the processing speed chosen, and watch the dashboard and email for requests for information.
Enter Ghana within 90 days of issue with the passport used to apply, the eVisa and the yellow fever certificate.
Declare anything prohibited or dutiable at customs.
For more than 90 days in a year, register for a Non-citizen Ghanacard with the National Identification Authority.

financial-infrastructure.summary: Official tax, banking and international-transfer infrastructure in Ghana.

facts.label: Tax authority
facts.text: Ghana Revenue Authority is the official national tax authority (or the official portal that publishes national tax rules). Tax residency, filing and any official non-resident rules should be read there.

facts.label: Central bank or financial regulator
facts.text: Bank of Ghana is the official central bank or a linked official financial regulator. Rules on accounts, payments and international transfers, where published, start there (and with licensed banks they supervise).

facts.label: Accounts and transfers
facts.text: Whether a non-resident can open a local bank account, and official tax-residency tests (often a published day-count plus other official ties), should be confirmed with the official tax authority and a licensed bank. International-transfer rules, including any official foreign-exchange controls, are those of the destination, not Australia.
